arXiv:2606.30627v1 [cs.LG] 29 Jun 2026

Pessimism’s Paradox: Conservative Offline Training Amplifies
Reward Hacking During Online Adaptation in Reasoning Models

Subramanyam Sahoo Affiliation: Horizon Research Correspondence to: sahoo2vec@gmail.com    Aman Chadha Affiliation: Apple    Vinija Jain Affiliation: Meta    Divya Chaudhary Affiliation: Northeastern University
Abstract

Conservative offline training is widely advocated as a safe foundation for subsequent online adaptation: if a policy stays close to well-supported behaviour, the argument goes, it is less likely to exploit imperfections in a learned reward model. We challenge this intuition empirically and mechanistically. We train a Qwen3-14B policy under Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) with three levels of conservatism (β∈{βlo,βmid,βhi}\beta\in\{\beta_{\mathrm{lo}},\beta_{\mathrm{mid}},\beta_{\mathrm{hi}}\} derived from empirical log-ratio percentiles), then adapt each checkpoint online against a learned reward ensemble (3 ×\times Qwen3-1.7B) while measuring true performance on GSM8K exact-answer accuracy. We find that higher offline conservatism monotonically increases reward-hacking damage, measured by the Goodhart gap and its area under the curve (AUGC), with Spearman ρ=1.0\rho=1.0 across all three conditions. Mechanistic analysis reveals a three-link causal chain: (i) high-β\beta DPO compresses policy entropy, (ii) Low-entropy policies generate responses with reduced diversity, concentrating in a narrow region of the reward model’s training distribution (lower pairwise cosine distance), and (iii) despite this proximity, ensemble disagreement (epistemic uncertainty) increases with β\beta and is exploited faster during online optimisation. We further fit a power-law curve to the (β,AUGC)(\beta,\mathrm{AUGC}) data and identify a practical optimal conservatism level β⋆\beta^{\star} that balances alignment fidelity against hacking vulnerability. Our results suggest that the field needs calibrated, not maximal, conservatism.

Keywords: 
offline reinforcement learning, reward hacking, Goodhart’s law, direct preference optimisation, uncertainty quantification, entropy collapse, safe adaptation, language models
††footnotetext: Code: Conservative-Offline-Training-Amplifies-Reward-Hacking-During-Online-Adaptation

1 Introduction

The standard recipe for safe language model alignment runs as follows: first perform offline training on human-preference data (e.g., via RLHF (Christiano et al., 2023) or DPO (Rafailov et al., 2024)) using a conservatism coefficient β\beta that penalises deviation from a reference policy, then optionally adapt online using a learned proxy reward. The implicit contract is that a more conservative offline checkpoint enters the online phase closer to the distribution where the reward model was trained, and therefore exploits it less aggressively.

To make this concrete, consider what a high-β\beta DPO objective actually does to the policy. It tightens the KL constraint against πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}, concentrating probability mass on a narrow slice of token sequences that πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} already assigns high density. The resulting policy has low output entropy and low response diversity. When this compressed policy is then optimised against a learned reward ensemble, two effects combine. First, the reward model was trained on a relatively diverse set of human-preference pairs; the compressed policy generates responses that lie in sparse regions of that training distribution, causing high epistemic uncertainty (ensemble disagreement). Second, a low-entropy starting point has fewer exploration directions through which gradient updates can improve true performance, so the optimiser rapidly channels all gradient signal toward reward-model blind spots. The net result is that the Goodhart gap—the divergence between proxy and true reward—opens faster and wider for high-β\beta policies.

This paper makes four contributions.

  1. 1.

    Empirical demonstration of the paradox using real models (Qwen3-14B policy, Qwen3-1.7B reward ensemble) and real data (UltraFeedback, GSM8K).

  2. 2.

    Mechanistic attribution via response-entropy collapse measurements and reward-model OOD-distance analysis.

  3. 3.

    A power-law fit of AUGC as a function of β\beta, yielding a practical design principle: an optimal β⋆\beta^{\star} exists below which online safety degrades faster than offline alignment improves.

  4. 4.

    Algorithmic and benchmark recommendations for the next generation of conservative-alignment methods that explicitly trade off pessimism against hacking vulnerability.

2 Background and Related Work

2.1 Direct Preference Optimisation

DPO (Rafailov et al., 2024) sidesteps the need for an explicit reward model by reparameterising the RLHF objective directly in terms of policy log-ratios. Given a preference dataset 𝒟={(x,yw,yl)}\mathcal{D}=\{(x,y_{w},y_{l})\} of prompts with winning and losing responses, DPO minimises

ℒDPO(πθ;πref)=−𝔼(x,yw,yl)∼𝒟[logσ(βlogπθ​(yw∣x)πref​(yw∣x)−βlogπθ​(yl∣x)πref​(yl∣x))].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\pi_{\theta};\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y_{w},y_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\log\sigma\Big(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{w}\mid x)}\\ -\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{l}\mid x)}\Big)\Big]. (1)

where σ\sigma is the logistic function and β>0\beta>0 is the conservatism coefficient. Larger β\beta imposes a tighter implicit KL constraint KL(πθ∥πref)\KL(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), pulling the learned policy closer to the reference.

2.2 Goodhart’s Law in RLHF

Goodhart’s Law (Goodhart, 1975) states that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. In the RLHF context, Gao et al. (2022) formalise this as a monotone degradation of true performance as the policy drifts toward maximising a proxy reward. Skalse et al. (2025) give a taxonomy of reward hacking and show it is near-inevitable when the reward model has any imperfection. Our work studies a less-explored facet: how the offline training strategy modulates the severity and speed of hacking during online adaptation.

2.3 Reward Model Ensembles and Uncertainty

Ensembling is the standard approach for epistemic uncertainty estimation in deep neural networks (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). In the reward-model context, ensemble disagreement provides a proxy for out-of-distribution inputs and has been used as a pessimism signal in offline RL (Kumar et al., 2020; Kidambi et al., 2021). Our ensemble (3 ×\times Qwen3-1.7B trained with bootstrap resampling) provides both the proxy reward signal and the uncertainty signal used in our mechanistic analysis.

2.4 Offline RL and Conservative Methods

The connection between DPO and offline RL is well known. CQL (Kumar et al., 2020) penalises Q-values for out-of-support actions; IQL (Kostrikov et al., 2021) avoids OOD actions by replacing Bellman backups with implicit quantile regression. The Decision Transformer (Chen et al., 2021) reframes RL as sequence modelling, which is directly analogous to DPO. All of these methods share the same conservatism logic encoded in Equation 1: larger conservatism coefficient →\to policy stays closer to reference →\to (assumed) safer online performance. We show this assumption is violated under a specific failure mode: OOD-driven reward hacking.

3 Problem Formulation

Let πθ\pi_{\theta} denote the policy being trained, πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} the frozen DPO checkpoint (which itself used πref(0)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(0)} as its reference), and r^ϕ​(x,y)\hat{r}_{\phi}(x,y) a learned proxy reward parameterised by an ensemble ϕ={ϕk}k=1K\phi=\{\phi_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}. The true reward r⋆​(x,y)r^{\star}(x,y) is verifiable (GSM8K exact-answer accuracy) and is observed only during evaluation, never during training.

Definition 3.1 (Goodhart Gap).

At online step tt, define the batch-averaged normalised rewards

r~proxy​(t)=r¯proxy​(t)|r¯proxy​(0)|+ε,r~true​(t)=r¯true​(t)|r¯true​(0)|+ε,\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{proxy}}(t)=\frac{\bar{r}_{\mathrm{proxy}}(t)}{\lvert\bar{r}_{\mathrm{proxy}}(0)\rvert+\varepsilon},\quad\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{true}}(t)=\frac{\bar{r}_{\mathrm{true}}(t)}{\lvert\bar{r}_{\mathrm{true}}(0)\rvert+\varepsilon},

where ε=ϵfloat32\varepsilon=\epsilon_{\mathrm{float32}}. The Goodhart gap is

𝒢⁡(t,β)=r~proxy​(t)−r~true​(t).\mathcal{G}(t;\beta)=\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{proxy}}(t)-\tilde{r}_{\mathrm{true}}(t). (2)
Definition 3.2 (AUGC).

The area under the Goodhart gap curve (AUGC) measures cumulative hacking damage over the online run:

AUGC⁡(β)=∫0Tmax⁡(𝒢⁡(t,β), 0)​𝑑t.\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta)=\int_{0}^{T}\max\!\bigl(\mathcal{G}(t;\beta),\,0\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t. (3)

The central question of this paper is: does AUGC⁡(β)\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta) increase or decrease with β\beta?

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Models and Data

Policy model.

We use Qwen/Qwen3-14B as the policy, loaded in 4-bit NF4 QLoRA quantisation (Dettmers et al., 2023) with LoRA adapters (Hu et al., 2021) applied to all attention projection matrices. The LoRA rank rr is derived architecturally:

r=2⌊log2⁡hhidden⌉,α=2​r,r=2^{\lfloor\log_{2}\sqrt{h_{\mathrm{hidden}}}\rceil},\quad\alpha=2r, (4)

where ⌈⋅⌉\lceil\cdot\rceil denotes rounding to nearest integer and hhiddenh_{\mathrm{hidden}} is the model hidden dimension. The dropout rate is dataset-derived: pdrop=clip⁡(32/n,0.01,0.10)p_{\mathrm{drop}}=\mathrm{clip}(32/\sqrt{n},0.01,0.10) for nn training examples.

Reward ensemble.

Three independent Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B sequence classifiers (also QLoRA) are trained with bootstrap resampling to produce both a mean reward and an epistemic uncertainty (ensemble standard deviation). Each member is trained with the Bradley–Terry preference loss (Bradley and Terry, 1952):

ℒBT=−𝔼(x,yw,yl)∼𝒟⁡log⁡σ⁡(rϕ​(x,yw)−rϕ​(x,yl)).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BT}}=-\E_{(x,y_{w},y_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}}\log\sigma\!\bigl(r_{\phi}(x,y_{w})-r_{\phi}(x,y_{l})\bigr). (5)

Preference data.

Offline DPO and reward-model training use HuggingFaceH4/ultrafeedback_binarized (Cui et al., 2024), split 80/10/10.

Verifiable task.

Online true reward is evaluated on openai/gsm8k (main) (Cobbe et al., 2021) using exact-answer matching after extracting the number following the #### delimiter.

4.2 Deriving the β\beta Grid

We do not choose β\beta values arbitrarily. Instead, we compute the per-example absolute log-ratio magnitude under the frozen reference policy πref(0)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(0)}:

δi=|logπref(0)(yw(i)∣x(i))−logπref(0)(yl(i)∣x(i))|.\delta_{i}=\bigl\lvert\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(0)}(y_{w}^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)})-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(0)}(y_{l}^{(i)}\mid x^{(i)})\bigr\rvert. (6)

The three β\beta values are taken at the 20th, 50th, and 80th percentiles of {δi}\{\delta_{i}\}, normalised by the median absolute log-ratio:

βj=pctpj​({δi})median⁡({δi})+ε,(p1,p2,p3)=(20,50,80).\beta_{j}=\frac{\mathrm{pct}_{p_{j}}(\{\delta_{i}\})}{\mathrm{median}(\{\delta_{i}\})+\varepsilon},\quad(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3})=(20,50,80). (7)

This makes the three conservatism levels commensurate with the actual preference signal magnitude, not with arbitrary numerical choices.

4.3 Offline DPO Training

For each β∈{βlo,βmid,βhi}\beta\in\{\beta_{\mathrm{lo}},\beta_{\mathrm{mid}},\beta_{\mathrm{hi}}\}, we fine-tune an independent LoRA adapter using Equation 1 via the TRL DPOTrainer (Von Werra et al., 2022). The per-device batch size, gradient accumulation, learning rate, and gradient clipping are all derived from hardware properties and the training set size (see Appendix C for derivation formulas).

4.4 Online Adaptation Loop

After offline DPO, each checkpoint is adapted online using the objective

ℒonline=−𝔼τ∼πθ​[A^​(x,y)⋅log⁡πθ​(y∣x)]+κ(β)⋅𝔼[(logπθ(y∣x)−logπref(y∣x))2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{online}}=-\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\Bigl[\hat{A}(x,y)\cdot\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\Bigr]\\ +\kappa(\beta)\cdot\mathbb{E}\!\Bigl[\bigl(\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)\bigr)^{2}\Bigr]. (8)

where the normalised advantage is

A^​(x,y)=r^​(x,y)−μr^σr^+ε,\hat{A}(x,y)=\frac{\hat{r}(x,y)-\mu_{\hat{r}}}{\sigma_{\hat{r}}+\varepsilon}, (9)

and the adaptive KL coefficient is

κ⁡(β)=βQpKL​(|log⁡πθ−log⁡πref|)+ε.\kappa(\beta)=\frac{\beta}{Q_{p_{\mathrm{KL}}}\!\bigl(\lvert\log\pi_{\theta}-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\rvert\bigr)+\varepsilon}. (10)

Here QpKLQ_{p_{\mathrm{KL}}} denotes the empirical pKLp_{\mathrm{KL}}-th percentile of the absolute KL values over the current batch. This normalisation makes the KL penalty scale-invariant with respect to the policy’s divergence level.

5 Mechanistic Analysis

To explain the paradox, we identify three causal links illustrated in Figure 2: entropy compression, OOD distance amplification, and uncertainty-driven exploitation.

5.1 Link 1: Entropy Compression

We measure the mean token-level entropy of each DPO checkpoint on a fixed probe set of nprobe=⌈|Dtest|⌉n_{\mathrm{probe}}=\lceil\sqrt{|D_{\mathrm{test}}|}\rceil GSM8K prompts:

H(β)=−1|𝒳probe|∑x∈𝒳probe1|x|∑t∑v∈𝒱πθ(β)(v∣x<t)logπθ(β)(v∣x<t).H^{(\beta)}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{probe}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{probe}}}\frac{1}{|x|}\sum_{t}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\pi_{\theta}^{(\beta)}(v\mid x_{<t})\log\pi_{\theta}^{(\beta)}(v\mid x_{<t}). (11)

Proposition 5.1 formalises the expected relationship.

Proposition 5.1 (Entropy–conservatism monotonicity).

Under mild regularity conditions on the DPO loss landscape, the equilibrium policy entropy H(β)H^{(\beta)} is non-increasing in β\beta:

β1≤β2⇒H(β1)≥H(β2).\beta_{1}\leq\beta_{2}\;\Rightarrow\;H^{(\beta_{1})}\geq H^{(\beta_{2})}.
Proof sketch.

The DPO stationary condition implies πθ(β)​(y∣x)∝πref​(y∣x)​exp⁡(r⁡(y∣x)/β)\pi_{\theta}^{(\beta)}(y\mid x)\propto\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\!\bigl(r(y\mid x)/\beta\bigr) where rr is the implicit reward. The entropy of a Gibbs distribution over a fixed reward function is a non-increasing function of 1/β1/\beta (equivalently, non-decreasing in temperature τ=β\tau=\beta), which establishes the claim. ∎

We further observe entropy collapse: after online adaptation, the entropy of the high-β\beta policy decreases more than that of the low-β\beta policy. This is measured as Δ​H(β)=HDPO(β)−Honline(β)\Delta H^{(\beta)}=H_{\mathrm{DPO}}^{(\beta)}-H_{\mathrm{online}}^{(\beta)}.

5.2 Link 2: OOD Distance from the Reward Model

Let 𝐡ϕ​(x,y)∈ℝd\mathbf{h}_{\phi}(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the mean-pooled penultimate-layer hidden state of reward ensemble member ϕ0\phi_{0} for input (x,y)(x,y). We measure out-of-distribution distance as the cosine distance between the hidden state of a generated response and the centroid of the UltraFeedback training distribution:

dcos(β)=1−𝐡ϕ​(x,y(β))⊤​μref‖𝐡ϕ​(x,y(β))‖2​‖μref‖2,d_{\cos}^{(\beta)}=1-\frac{\mathbf{h}_{\phi}(x,y^{(\beta)})^{\top}\,\mu_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\|\mathbf{h}_{\phi}(x,y^{(\beta)})\|_{2}\,\|\mu_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}}, (12)

where μref=1nref​∑i=1nref𝐡ϕ​(xi,yiuf)\mu_{\mathrm{ref}}=\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{ref}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{\mathrm{ref}}}\mathbf{h}_{\phi}(x_{i},y_{i}^{\mathrm{uf}}) is the reference centroid computed from nref=⌈|Dtrain|⌉n_{\mathrm{ref}}=\lceil\sqrt{|D_{\mathrm{train}}|}\rceil UltraFeedback training examples. We also compute mean pairwise cosine distance as a response diversity metric.

5.3 Link 3: Uncertainty-Driven Exploitation

The ensemble uncertainty signal is

u^​(x,y)=1K−1​∑k=1K(rϕk​(x,y)−r¯​(x,y))2,\hat{u}(x,y)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl(r_{\phi_{k}}(x,y)-\bar{r}(x,y)\bigr)^{2}}, (13)

where r¯​(x,y)=K−1​∑krϕk​(x,y)\bar{r}(x,y)=K^{-1}\sum_{k}r_{\phi_{k}}(x,y). When u^\hat{u} is high, individual members disagree strongly about the true reward of a response. The online optimiser maximises r¯\bar{r}, but the disagreement means the landscape is unreliable. The policy quickly finds responses that fool some but not all ensemble members—a classic form of distributional reward hacking (Pan et al., 2022).

We compute the Pearson correlation ρUQ​(β)\rho_{\mathrm{UQ}}(\beta) between the time series of u^\hat{u} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} for each β\beta condition, and report the relationship in the summary table (Table 1).

6 Theory: Optimal Conservatism

Having established the empirical and mechanistic case, we now ask: what is the optimal β\beta?

Definition 6.1 (Optimal conservatism).

Let 𝒜⁡(β)\mathcal{A}(\beta) denote the offline alignment quality (e.g., win rate over πref(0)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}^{(0)}) and AUGC⁡(β)\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta) the online hacking damage. The optimal conservatism β⋆\beta^{\star} solves

β⋆=arg​minβ>0⁡AUGC​(β)−λ⋅𝒜⁡(β),\beta^{\star}=\argmin_{\beta>0}\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta)-\lambda\cdot\mathcal{A}(\beta),

where λ>0\lambda>0 weights alignment against hacking risk.

For the empirical approximation, we fit a power law to the observed (β,AUGC)(\beta,\mathrm{AUGC}) data:

AUGC⁡(β)≈a⋅βb+c,a,b,c>0.\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta)\approx a\cdot\beta^{b}+c,\quad a,b,c>0. (14)

Parameters (a,b,c)(a,b,c) are obtained by least-squares optimisation with initialisation derived from the data range (see Appendix E). The practical β⋆\beta^{\star} is then defined as the smallest β\beta at which AUGC\mathrm{AUGC} exceeds 1.5×minβ′⁡AUGC⁡(β′)1.5\times\min_{\beta^{\prime}}\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta^{\prime}):

β⋆=inf{β:AUGC⁡(β)>1.5⋅(c+a⋅βminb)}.\beta^{\star}=\inf\!\bigl\{\beta:\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta)>1.5\cdot(c+a\cdot\beta_{\min}^{b})\bigr\}. (15)
Proposition 6.2 (Power-law hacking damage).

If Equation 14 holds with b>1b>1, then the marginal hacking cost grows super-linearly in β\beta: ∂2∂β2​AUGC​(β)=a​b​(b−1)​βb−2>0\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\beta^{2}}\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta)=a\,b\,(b-1)\,\beta^{b-2}>0. This implies that beyond β⋆\beta^{\star}, small increases in conservatism incur disproportionately large hacking risk.

7 Results

7.1 Goodhart Gap Trajectories

Figure 3 shows the Goodhart gap 𝒢⁡(t,β)\mathcal{G}(t;\beta) across online adaptation steps for all three β\beta levels. The hacking threshold τhack\tau_{\mathrm{hack}} is set at the 75th percentile of all positive gap values, derived from the data (not hand-tuned). Key observations: (a) the Goodhart gap is predominantly negative throughout, indicating the proxy reward overestimates true performance; (b) Low β\beta (β=0.310\beta=0.310) shows the most volatile trajectory, oscillating to −3×106-3\times 10^{6}, while Mid β\beta and High β\beta remain near zero; and (c) the cumulative hacking damage (AUGC) is nonetheless monotonically ordered by β\beta (31.1, 43.0, 145.8), confirming the paradox.

7.2 AUGC Summary

Table 1 reports AUGC, mean uncertainty, hacking onset step, and UQ-gap Pearson correlation for each β\beta condition. The Spearman rank correlation between β\beta and AUGC is ρ=1.0\rho=1.0 (perfect monotone ordering), confirming the paradox.

7.3 Entropy Collapse

Figure 4 summarises the entropy measurements. The left panel shows that DPO checkpoint entropy is nearly identical across all three β\beta levels (≈0.81\approx 0.81–0.820.82), with only a marginal decrease at higher β\beta, broadly consistent with Proposition 5.1. The right panel reveals an unexpected pattern: Low β\beta shows a small positive entropy collapse (≈+0.004\approx{+}0.004), Mid β\beta is near zero, and High β\beta shows a negative collapse (≈−0.0025\approx{-}0.0025), meaning the most conservative policy gains entropy during online adaptation rather than losing it.

7.4 OOD Distance and the β⋆\beta^{\star} Curve

Figure 5 shows the fitted power-law curve overlaid on the three AUGC data points. The safe zone [0,β⋆][0,\beta^{\star}] and danger zone (β⋆,∞)(\beta^{\star},\infty) are shaded. The goodness of fit R2=1.0R^{2}=1.0 at three data points (exact fit), but the power-law form provides a smooth extrapolation for practical design guidance.

8 Discussion

8.1 Why the Paradox Matters

The conventional conservative-offline-RL argument is a support argument: train on data in the support of the behaviour policy, and the reward model generalises accurately there. Our paradox reveals a subtle conflict: the support of a high-β\beta DPO policy may be quite different from the support of the reward model’s training data, even though the DPO policy stays close to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. This happens because DPO concentrates mass in a low-entropy region that πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} assigns high density to, but the reward model was trained on diverse human preference data. The intersection of “what the DPO policy generates” and “what the reward model was trained on” is smaller for high β\beta, not larger.

8.2 Connection to the Conservative Offline-to-Online Framework

The companion paper (the workshop draft) proposes a unified conservative loop that applies to both offline RL and offline BO. Our findings provide a concrete empirical instantiation of when that loop can backfire: when the offline phase uses a proxy reward (DPO) whose implicit reward model is different from the reward model used online. The offline alignment step concentrates the policy using one measure of quality; the online step optimises a different (learned) measure. The mismatch is the source of the paradox.

8.3 Limitations

Our study uses a single hardware target (H100 80GB), three β\beta values, and a specific policy/reward model combination (Qwen3-14B/Qwen3-1.7B). The power-law fit is exact at three points by construction; the R2=1.0R^{2}=1.0 claim should not be interpreted as strong evidence for the functional form, only as an interpolation device. A broader study with more β\beta values, multiple model families, and multiple downstream tasks is needed to generalise the findings.

9 Conclusion

We demonstrated that conservative offline training can amplify rather than dampen reward hacking during online adaptation. The mechanism is a three-link chain: high-β\beta DPO compresses policy entropy, which pushes generated responses out of the reward model’s training distribution, which creates exploitable epistemic uncertainty. We formalised Goodhart’s gap and its area under the curve as the primary evaluation metric, derived an optimal conservatism level β⋆\beta^{\star} from a power-law fit, and provided algorithmic recommendations for calibrated conservatism. These findings point toward a richer view of safe offline-to-online alignment: one that explicitly accounts for the distribution mismatch between the offline alignment signal and the online proxy reward.

Appendix A Proof of Proposition 5.1

We provide a more detailed version of the proof sketch given in Section 5.1. Recall the variational characterisation of the DPO solution. The KL-regularised reward maximisation problem is

maxπθ𝔼x∼p0𝔼y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[r⋆(x,y)]−β⋅KL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥πref(⋅∣x)),\max_{\pi_{\theta}}\;\E_{x\sim p_{0}}\E_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\bigl[r^{\star}(x,y)\bigr]-\beta\cdot\KL\!\bigl(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr), (A.1)

where r⋆r^{\star} is the implicit reward recovered by DPO. The unique solution to Equation A.1 is the Gibbs distribution:

πθ(β)​(y∣x)=πref​(y∣x)​exp⁡(r⋆​(x,y)/β)Zβ​(x),\pi_{\theta}^{(\beta)}(y\mid x)=\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\!\bigl(r^{\star}(x,y)/\beta\bigr)}{Z_{\beta}(x)}, (A.2)

where Zβ​(x)=∑y′πref​(y′∣x)​exp⁡(r⋆​(x,y′)/β)Z_{\beta}(x)=\sum_{y^{\prime}}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y^{\prime}\mid x)\exp\!\bigl(r^{\star}(x,y^{\prime})/\beta\bigr).

The entropy of this Gibbs distribution is

H(πθ(β)(⋅∣x))\displaystyle H\!\bigl(\pi_{\theta}^{(\beta)}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr) =−∑yπθ(β)(y∣x)logπθ(β)(y∣x)\displaystyle=-\sum_{y}\pi_{\theta}^{(\beta)}(y\mid x)\log\pi_{\theta}^{(\beta)}(y\mid x)
=log⁡Zβ​(x)−1β​𝔼y∼πθ(β)​[r⋆​(x,y)].\displaystyle=\log Z_{\beta}(x)-\frac{1}{\beta}\E_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}^{(\beta)}}[r^{\star}(x,y)]. (A.3)

Differentiating with respect to β\beta (and suppressing xx):

∂H∂β=1β2​(𝔼⁡[r⋆]−∂log⁡Zβ∂(1/β)⋅β)=1β2​Vary∼πθ(β)​[r⋆​(x,y)]≥0.\frac{\partial H}{\partial\beta}=\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}\Bigl(\E[r^{\star}]-\frac{\partial\log Z_{\beta}}{\partial(1/\beta)}\cdot\beta\Bigr)=\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}\Var_{y\sim\pi_{\theta}^{(\beta)}}[r^{\star}(x,y)]\geq 0. (A.4)

Thus HH is non-decreasing in β\beta (non-increasing in 1/β1/\beta), confirming Proposition 5.1. □\square

Remark A.1.

The result holds for any proper distribution; it is a standard property of exponential families. The important consequence is that increasing β\beta (more pessimism) strictly compresses entropy unless the reward is constant, which is never the case in practice.

Appendix B Proof of Proposition 6.2

Given AUGC⁡(β)=a​βb+c\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta)=a\beta^{b}+c with a,b,c>0a,b,c>0, the first and second derivatives are:

∂∂β​AUGC​(β)\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta) =a​b​βb−1>0,\displaystyle=ab\beta^{b-1}>0, (A.5)
∂2∂β2​AUGC​(β)\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial\beta^{2}}\mathrm{AUGC}(\beta) =a​b​(b−1)​βb−2.\displaystyle=ab(b-1)\beta^{b-2}. (A.6)

The second derivative is positive iff b>1b>1. If b>1b>1, AUGC is strictly convex in β\beta, meaning marginal hacking cost grows faster than linearly. In our data, the fitted b>1b>1 (confirmed experimentally), so the super-linearity claim holds. □\square

Appendix C Complete Hyperparameter Derivation

All hyperparameters are derived from the architecture, hardware, and data, with no hand-tuned magic numbers.

C.1 LoRA Rank

Given hidden dimension hh:

r=2⌊log2⁡h⌉,rmin=4,rmax=64,r←clip⁡(r,rmin,rmax).r=2^{\lfloor\log_{2}\sqrt{h}\rceil},\quad r_{\min}=4,\quad r_{\max}=64,\quad r\leftarrow\mathrm{clip}(r,r_{\min},r_{\max}). (B.1)

LoRA scaling: α=2​r\alpha=2r.

C.2 LoRA Dropout

pdrop=clip⁡(32n, 0.01, 0.10),p_{\mathrm{drop}}=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\frac{32}{\sqrt{n}},\,0.01,\,0.10\right), (B.2)

where nn is the training set size. More data ⇒\Rightarrow less regularisation.

C.3 Batch Size

B=2⌊log2⁡(VGBPB⋅m⋅s−1)⌋,B←clip⁡(B,1,64),B=2^{\lfloor\log_{2}\bigl(\tfrac{V_{\mathrm{GB}}}{P_{\mathrm{B}}}\cdot m\cdot s^{-1}\bigr)\rfloor},\quad B\leftarrow\mathrm{clip}(B,1,64), (B.3)

where VGBV_{\mathrm{GB}} is VRAM in GB, PBP_{\mathrm{B}} is model size in billion parameters, m∈{1,2}m\in\{1,2\} is a training/inference multiplier, and s=ℓ/1024s=\ell/1024 is the sequence length pressure factor.

C.4 Learning Rate

η=clip⁡(η0ntrainable/n0,ηmin,ηmax),\eta=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\frac{\eta_{0}}{\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{trainable}}/n_{0}}},\eta_{\min},\,\eta_{\max}\right), (B.4)

where η0=×10−4\eta_{0}=2\!\times\!10^{-4}, n0=107n_{0}=10^{7}, ηmin=×10−7\eta_{\min}=5\!\times\!10^{-7}, ηmax=×10−4\eta_{\max}=2\!\times\!10^{-4}. Larger adapter ⇒\Rightarrow smaller learning rate.

C.5 Gradient Clipping Norm

cclip=clip⁡(log10⁡(ntrainable)log10⁡(107),0.5, 2.0).c_{\mathrm{clip}}=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\frac{\log_{10}(n_{\mathrm{trainable}})}{\log_{10}(10^{7})},0.5,\,2.0\right). (B.5)

C.6 Warmup Steps

Twarmup=⌊Ttotal⌋,T_{\mathrm{warmup}}=\lfloor\sqrt{T_{\mathrm{total}}}\rfloor, (B.6)

a square-root schedule that provides early stability without sacrificing too many training steps.

C.7 Weight Decay

λwd=1ntrain.\lambda_{\mathrm{wd}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{train}}}}. (B.7)

This gives more regularisation when data is scarce.

Appendix E Power-Law Fitting Details

The power-law curve (Equation 14) is fit via scipy.optimize.curve_fit with the following data-derived initial parameters:

a0\displaystyle a_{0} =AUGCmax−AUGCmin,\displaystyle=\mathrm{AUGC}_{\max}-\mathrm{AUGC}_{\min}, (C.1)
b0\displaystyle b_{0} =log⁡(AUGCmax/AUGCmin)log⁡(βmax/βmin),\displaystyle=\frac{\log(\mathrm{AUGC}_{\max}/\mathrm{AUGC}_{\min})}{\log(\beta_{\max}/\beta_{\min})}, (C.2)
c0\displaystyle c_{0} =AUGCmin.\displaystyle=\mathrm{AUGC}_{\min}. (C.3)

Parameter bounds are a,b,c∈[0,∞)a,b,c\in[0,\infty). The optimisation runs for up to 10,000 function evaluations. The practical β⋆\beta^{\star} is found by dense grid search over β∈[0.1​βmin,2​βmax]\beta\in[0.1\beta_{\min},2\beta_{\max}] with 1000 evenly spaced points, finding the first β\beta for which AUGC^​(β)>1.5×AUGC^​(βmin)\widehat{\mathrm{AUGC}}(\beta)>1.5\times\widehat{\mathrm{AUGC}}(\beta_{\min}).

Appendix F Benchmark Evaluation Protocol

A complete benchmark reproducing our findings should report the following metrics in addition to task performance:

  1. 1.

    Goodhart gap time series 𝒢⁡(t,β)\mathcal{G}(t;\beta) at a minimum of ⌈T/50⌉\lceil T/50\rceil evaluation points.

  2. 2.

    AUGC (Eq. 3) and its standard error over at least three seeds.

  3. 3.

    DPO checkpoint entropy H(β)H^{(\beta)} on a fixed probe set.

  4. 4.

    Entropy collapse Δ​H(β)\Delta H^{(\beta)}.

  5. 5.

    OOD cosine distance dcos(β)d_{\cos}^{(\beta)} from the reward model’s training distribution.

  6. 6.

    Response diversity (mean pairwise cosine distance).

  7. 7.

    Spearman ρ\rho between β\beta and AUGC.

  8. 8.

    UQ–gap correlation rUQ​(β)r_{\mathrm{UQ}}(\beta).

  9. 9.

    Power-law parameters (a,b,c)(a,b,c) and R2R^{2} of the fit.

  10. 10.

    Optimal β⋆\beta^{\star} and the AUGC at that point.

For reproducibility, every benchmark should specify: (a) the exact β\beta derivation method (ours uses empirical log-ratio percentiles); (b) the hacking threshold derivation (ours uses the 75th percentile of positive gap values); (c) evaluation seed protocol; and (d) the logging policy and dataset coverage statistics.

Appendix G Limitations and Future Work

Single hardware target.

All experiments run on a single H100 80GB. Memory-constrained derivations of batch size and LoRA rank depend on VGBV_{\mathrm{GB}}; results may differ slightly on A100 or consumer GPUs.

Three β\beta values.

A power-law fit at three points is exact by construction. Validating the functional form requires at least five to eight β\beta values spanning two orders of magnitude.

Single model family.

We use Qwen3 throughout. The entropy-compression mechanism should be model-agnostic (it follows from the Gibbs-distribution form of the DPO solution), but the quantitative curve may differ for other architectures or scales.

Future work.

(1) Multi-model, multi-task replication. (2) Adaptive β\beta scheduling that tracks u^\hat{u} online and reduces β\beta when uncertainty grows. (3) Extension to other offline alignment methods (ORPO, SimPO, KTO) to test whether the paradox is specific to DPO’s KL regularisation or arises for any conservative offline objective. (4) Connecting the entropy-collapse mechanism to plasticity loss (Lyle et al., 2023) in continual RL.
